newsitem.title: USA: Montana governor, Clinton discuss bison problem.
newsitem.headline: Montana governor, Clinton discuss bison problem.

text.p: Montana Gov. Marc Racicot said Wednesday he discussed with President Clinton his state's demands to control bison ranging out of Yellowstone National Park that ranchers fear could spread disease to cattle.

Racicot said Clinton brought the issue up at the National Governors Conference here this week and he had met with White House environmental adviser Katy McGinty and Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman on the issue.

But he said in a telephone news conference from Montana he did not see a quick resolution to the problem that has prompted the shooting this winter of more than 700 bison from the Yellowstone herd that used to number more than 3,000.
"Nothing solidified came out of this discussion," Racicot said, noting that Glickman indicated he might visit the area to evaluate the problem first-hand.

An Agriculture Department agency, the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, has threatened to pull Montana's status as a brucellosis-free state if the bison, some of which are infected with the disease, get out of the park onto surrounding grazing lands. Because of this buffalo have been shot in record numbers as they left the park for lower lands in search of food during this unusually harsh winter.

Brucellosis, which has little effect on buffalo, causes cattle to spontaneously abort calves and to produce less milk. APHIS has conducted a costly programme over a number of years to all but eradicate the disease in U.S. cattle.

Environmentalists contend that APHIS is being unreasonable by barring bison from setting foot on the grazing lands, however, as there are no documented cases of the disease being transmitted in the wild from bison to cattle.
Racicot said Montana has pushed federal agencies to determine how many bison the park's ecosystem can maintain, then move the rest to a quarantine area.

Those that are infected should be slaughtered, he said, while healthy bison should be moved to another area. He also said there have been at least a few offers from landowners to maintain buffalo elsewhere in the state.

"We could find an appropriate facility where you could maintain the integrity of your domestic livestock industry, where you could assure that there would be aboslutely no disease transmission whatsoever and where you could bring back a very healthy population of bison both in the park and in this particular facility," Racicot said.
